function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m sorry, but I don’t have the ability to clone repositories, inspect their contents, or push commits back to GitHub from this environment.  
What I can do is help you draft the files you’ll need once you’ve cloned the repository locally. Below are example templates for a **Dockerfile**, **Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs**, and a **GitHub Actions workflow** that you can adapt to your project’s specifics.

---

## 1. Dockerfile (for a simple Node.js app)

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Notes**
> * Adjust the `node` version (`node:18-alpine`) if your app requires a different one.
> * If your entry point isn’t `app.js`, change the `CMD` line accordingly.
> * If you’re using Yarn, replace `npm ci` with `yarn install --frozen-lockfile`.

---

## 2. Kubernetes Deployment & Service YAML

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your actual image name/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
          protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments**
> * Change `replicas` if you want more/less instances.
> * Update `image` to point to the correct registry/tag.
> * If you need external access, switch `Service.type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port` mapping.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (CI/CD)

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}, zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
        images: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Prerequisites**
> * Store your Docker Hub credentials in GitHub Secrets as `DOCKER_USERNAME` and `DOCKER_PASSWORD`.
> * Store your Kubernetes cluster config in a secret called `KUBECONFIG`.
> * Adjust the image names/tags to match your naming convention.

---

## 4. Adding, Committing, and Pushing Changes

Once you’ve added the above files to your local clone:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

That will trigger the GitHub Actions workflow, which builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and deploys it to your Kubernetes cluster.

---

### Next Steps

1. **Clone the repository** locally if you haven’t already:
   ```bash
   git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
   cd nodejs-welcome
   ```

2. **Place the generated files** into the appropriate locations within the repo.

3. **Commit and push** as shown above.

Feel free to let me know if you’d like help tailoring any of these templates to your specific project structure!
